Is there some sort of compendium/good book/hadith of official, cannon information given out by the game developers/loremasters? How much of what we know is speculation/connecting of the dots?
What primary sources does Elder Scrolls lore come from outside of the games?

There are hundreds of books in the games -- these, plus the events and dialog of the games themselves, make up most of the canon. Check the references section of articles on UESPWiki.

Of course, you can't necessarily trust every book you read or the NPCs you talk with -- which makes it more like a real, unreliable history than an official canonical universe.

Oh yes, the books and books and books, I almost forgot how many of those there are and how much they cover. Never read too many when playing through the games. I love the idea of not being able to trust the histories found in the game. It makes me think of the early historians that had crazy ideas that twisted the past to match the thinking of the time, like the Roman Empire falling because its people became morally corrupt, or that history could be cleanly divided into Golden, Silver, Bronze, and Iron ages of Ovid.

The Greg Keyes novels were written with lots of Bethesda involvement, ESO has lore wares available (Hero's Guide to Tamriel, etc.) Some of the developers are also active to varying degrees on the forums, including a very large and well-known dev/fan roleplay on BGSF (The Trial of Vivec) and giving interviews in and out of character.

Depending on your opinion of the validity of Michael Kirkbride's opinions on TES (worked on Daggerfall, Redguard, and Morrowind, wrote lots of the Tribunal and the 36 Lessons of Vivec) after his departure from Bethesda, his C0DA story and other texts are also a pretty enormous source of both information and contention.

Side note: MK was active on /r/teslore for a time, has dumped a rather large amount of information on us there (midway down /r/myrrlyn are four logs of IRC chats he had with us), and his fiancé is LadyNerevar, the primary curator of The Imperial Library. In addition to his contributions on personal time, he was also a contract writer for Oblivion, especially KotN, and his out-of-game texts were referenced in both Skyrim and ESO.

A staggering amount of the information many scholars tend to take for granted is the result of dot-connecting of various pieces of raw information scattered throughout the series that is either supported or just not contradicted so far. The information ESO provides is also still being digested, and has some really crazy stuff like Water as Memory. We've also seen posts by various lore devs indicating that not only do they read the various fan communities, but they like the stuff produced and can't acknowledge it directly in-game for both legal and community reasons.

The Imperial Library, linked above, holds all in-game texts available for perusal, and UESP is an excellent encyclopedia of topics with generally well-cited summaries and explanations.

The games of course hold the lions' share of information, then the Keyes novels and developer interactions on communities make up the remnant of what can be considered "official" information. Community analysis, study, and creation has resulted in a whole new wealth of things that can freely be considered lore in the eyes of the beholder if they so choose, but that can at times be a fractious issue.
